**Why it matters:** NSO success rate is below 52% at 400 Elo gaps. Characterizing how chain length affects this supports principled design of nested oversight architectures.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight (April 2025); NSO ceiling on efficacy; compounding error accumulation.

# Asymmetric Debate: Does Giving the Truthful Debater Extra Resources Improve Truth-Seeking in Debate?

**Problem:** Standard debate gives both sides equal resources. Asymmetric debate (where the truthful side has more compute or better tools) might improve truth-convergence.

**Direction:** Implement asymmetric debate protocols (varying compute budget ratios between sides). Measure how truth-convergence rate changes as the advantage shifts from one side to the other.

**Why it matters:** If truth-seeking can be improved by asymmetric resource allocation, this is a practical design choice for oversight systems. This tests the theoretical prediction that truth has a structural advantage in debate.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight: Guards vs. Houdinis framework; debate protocols; compounding risks of oversight failure.

# Counterfactual Oversight Probing: What Would the Model Have Done Without the Overseer Signal?

**Problem:** Standard oversight measures what the model does under supervision, not the counterfactual (what it would have done without it). This makes it impossible to measure how much the oversight is actually changing behavior.

**Direction:** Train the same model in two conditions: with and without oversight. Compare behaviors on a shared test set. Measure the causal effect of oversight on model behavior distribution, not just the final accuracy.

**Why it matters:** The counterfactual effect of oversight is the true safety-relevant metric. A model that would behave identically without oversight is not being improved by the oversight at all.

**Relevant context:** Causal chain intervention; determining if models provide genuinely believed-correct responses.

# Population-Level Oversight vs. Individual-Level Oversight: Does Aggregate Oversight Quality Hide Critical Individual Failures?

**Problem:** Oversight quality metrics report averages. High average quality can coexist with systematic failure on a specific minority of critical cases. Identifying this distribution matters.

**Direction:** Measure oversight quality at the population level and then decompose by task subtype. Identify whether specific subtypes have disproportionately low oversight quality even when the aggregate metric is high.

**Why it matters:** Safety failures often come from tail cases where average metrics hide poor performance. Oversight quality must be evaluated at the subgroup level, not just in aggregate.

**Relevant context:** Safetywashing paper: benchmarks that do not distinguish harm severity levels; oversight error taxonomy.

# Oversight Sensitivity Analysis: Which Task Features Most Affect Oversight Quality?

**Problem:** Oversight quality varies across tasks, but the features that drive this variation are not understood. A systematic sensitivity analysis would identify which features are most predictive of oversight difficulty.

**Direction:** Collect a large set of tasks with known oversight quality. Train a regression model to predict oversight difficulty from task features (length, domain, reasoning type, ambiguity, etc.). Identify the strongest predictors.

**Why it matters:** If oversight difficulty can be predicted from task features, future oversight experiments can be designed to include coverage of all difficulty types and deployment systems can allocate oversight effort appropriately.

**Relevant context:** Tool/benchmark gap; oversight error taxonomy; easy-to-hard generalization.

# Oversight Quality Under Ambiguity: When Overseers Disagree, Who Is Right?

**Problem:** On ambiguous tasks, different overseers disagree. There is no principled method for determining which overseer is correct and whether any aggregation strategy produces a better signal than individual overseers.

**Direction:** Collect tasks where multiple overseers disagree. Use cases where ground truth is eventually determinable (e.g., predictions that resolve) to assess which overseer or aggregation strategy had the most accurate judgment.

**Why it matters:** Oversight of ambiguous tasks is especially important for AI safety (ethics, value judgments). Understanding how to aggregate disagreeing overseer judgments is an unsolved practical problem.

**Relevant context:** Quality-representativeness tradeoff; multi-reviewer oversight from peer review; overseer disagreement as signal.

# Skill-Based Overseer Routing: Directing Each Task to the Overseer With the Relevant Skill Set

**Problem:** No single overseer is best for all tasks. Routing tasks to overseers based on their specific skill profiles could improve aggregate oversight quality without requiring any overseer to improve.

**Direction:** Profile the skill sets of multiple weak overseers. Implement a routing system that assigns each task to the overseer with the best match. Compare aggregate oversight quality to using a single generalist overseer.

**Why it matters:** Skill-based routing is standard in organizational management (assigning work to the most qualified person). Applying it to AI oversight could be a practical quality improvement.

**Relevant context:** Cross-domain transfer from organizational management; specialization in oversight; ensemble oversight.

# Measurement Invariance Testing: Are Oversight Quality Metrics Consistent Across Task Domains?

**Problem:** A benchmark that measures oversight quality in one domain may measure a different construct in another domain. Measurement invariance testing (from psychometrics) would determine whether oversight quality metrics generalize across domains.

**Direction:** Apply measurement invariance testing to an oversight quality metric: measure whether the same metric captures the same construct across different task domains (factual, reasoning, evaluative). Report which comparisons are valid.

**Why it matters:** Without measurement invariance, comparisons of oversight quality across domains are invalid. This is a methodological prerequisite for the field.

**Relevant context:** Tool/benchmark gap: no standardized scalable oversight benchmarks; safetywashing paper on benchmark inconsistency.
